title: September 2026 - Liberty Street Economics
gist: This is a Liberty Street Economics monthly archive page listing a single September 2026 post, but it carries that post's full abstract: New York Fed regional business surveys find AI use jumped to more than 60 percent of service firms and about half of manufacturers (from 40 percent and 26 percent in 2025), while AI investment stays modest, usage is concentrated among few workers per firm, and layoffs remain uncommon. The stated conclusion is that firms are retraining workers rather than cutting them.

themes.theme: AI adoption rates in NY Fed regional business surveys

insights.claim: More than 60 percent of service firms and about half of manufacturers in the New York Fed's regional business surveys reported using AI in 2026, up from 40 percent and 26 percent respectively in 2025.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: Enterprise AI penetration is compounding fast off a mid-sized base, and services are running roughly a year ahead of manufacturing — supportive of software/AI seat-based demand, with manufacturing the later-cycle adoption leg.
insights.quote: AI use among regional businesses has continued to rise sharply, with more than 60 percent of service firms and about half of manufacturers now using AI—a notable increase from 40 percent and 26 percent, respectively, reported in 2025

insights.claim: Business AI spending is described as generally modest despite rising adoption, with usage concentrated among a small share of workers inside adopting firms.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: Headline adoption counts overstate monetizable AI spend: breadth of logos is not depth of budget, so watch seats-per-account and dollar-based expansion rather than adoption percentages.
insights.quote: regional firms’ investments in AI are generally modest, usage tends to be concentrated among a small share of workers within firms, and layoffs have remained uncommon

themes.theme: AI's labor-market impact: retraining rather than layoffs

insights.claim: Widespread AI adoption at regional firms has not produced widespread job cuts, with layoffs attributed to AI remaining uncommon across three years of survey data.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: Cuts against the mass-displacement narrative; argues against positioning for an AI-driven spike in unemployment claims in the near term.

insights.claim: AI's employment effect at firms is two-sided: some firms have scaled back hiring because of AI while others have added workers specifically to help deploy and use it.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: Net payroll effects can look flat while composition shifts — watch job-postings mix (AI-enablement roles up, generalist entry-level roles down) rather than aggregate headcount.
insights.quote: while some firms have scaled back hiring due to AI, others have added workers to help them use it

insights.claim: Retraining existing employees, not headcount reduction, is the primary way surveyed firms are adjusting their workforces in response to AI.
insights.speaker: NY Fed — Liberty Street Economics
insights.so_what: Points demand toward corporate training/upskilling and change-management services as an early AI-adjacent spend line, and implies AI shows up first as productivity per worker, not labor cost cuts.
insights.quote: Retraining employees in response to AI remains the primary way firms are adjusting their workforces.
